questions.question: Noted's activation is "created a document and returned within seven days." A revised signup flow shipped six weeks ago, and activation fell 11%. Which slot is most likely to explain a fall with no change in user behaviour?
options: Aggregation, because a rolling rate is more volatile than a cohort rate
Population, because the signup change alters who enters the denominator and when
Value link, because returning to the product was never the right outcome
Window, because seven days is too short to observe activation
questions.explanation: A signup change moves who is counted and at what moment they start being counted, so the number can drop with identical behaviour. Option C is true and irrelevant here: a weak value link makes the metric a poor target, but it does not produce a six-week movement.

questions.question: A PM proposes rebuilding the activation definition and restating the six-week trend on the new definition. What must be checked first?
options: Whether the team agrees the new definition is better than the old one
Whether the new number will be higher or lower than the old one
Whether the underlying events exist far enough back and carry every field the new definition needs
Whether the new definition uses the same seven-day window as the old one
questions.explanation: History can only be restated if the raw events support it. In Noted, actor identity is missing for about 18% of events, so a definition that depends on identifying the actor may not be computable historically at all. Option A is the tempting process answer: agreement about quality says nothing about whether the recomputation is possible.

questions.question: Which pairing gives the strongest protection against a metric being optimised without producing value?
options: Documents created per user, paired with total documents created
Documents created per user, paired with share of documents reopened after seven days
Documents created per user, paired with weekly active users
Documents created per user, paired with a stated target and an owner
questions.explanation: The cheapest way to raise document creation is to auto-create documents, and that path would push reopen rate down — so the counter-metric degrades exactly when the number is gamed. Option C is the standard pairing and fails: auto-creating documents does not reduce weekly active users, so the pair moves together under the cheap path.

questions.question: Noted's user-level activation is falling while workspace-level activation is flat. What is the most defensible reading?
options: One of the two numbers is computed incorrectly and should be reconciled
The workspace number should be preferred, since workspaces hold the paid seats
Activation is not really falling, since the two measures disagree
Both can be correct: they count different entities, so a shift in users per workspace would produce exactly this pattern
questions.explanation: The unit of the population is part of the metric's meaning, and two units can move in opposite directions truthfully at the same time. Option A is the instinct of a careful PM and it wastes the finding: treating the disagreement as a bug hides the mix shift that the disagreement is pointing at.

questions.question: A team writes a fully specified metric: population, event, window, aggregation, and aggregation unit are all unambiguous, and two analysts compute the same number. What has still not been established?
options: That the number stands in for a user outcome anyone cares about, and how that link could break
That the metric is comparable to industry benchmarks
That the metric will be stable over time
That the metric has an owner and a target
questions.explanation: Specification buys agreement, not relevance. A precisely defined number can be precisely disconnected from the job. Option C is tempting because stability sounds like the missing property — but a stable, well-defined, irrelevant metric is exactly the failure this boundary describes.
